plan.title: Hallmark signature scores: CD inflamed vs control ileum
plan.analytical_narrative:
The question is a per-sample score for every MSigDB hallmark signature across the 12 ileal biopsies (6 Crohn disease inflamed, 6 control) in counts.csv (12,000 genes x 12 samples, gene symbols, Salmon gene-level counts), plus a test of which signatures differ between the two conditions. It is a signature-scoring question, not a differential-expression or preranked-GSEA question, so nothing here fits a DE test or fgsea; the plan stays inside per-sample scoring and a test on the score matrix.

The user's own flag — 'one sample looks shallow' — matches the profile caveat that sample_01 has a library size about 4x below the median. That is handled in two places rather than by deletion: T1S1 keeps sample_01 through QC and reports its library size, detected genes, PCA position and distance-to-group beside the others, and T1S2 puts the depth difference inside the median-of-ratios size factors before the variance-stabilizing transform. Rank-based scoring (UCell, singscore) is additionally depth-robust by construction, since ranks within a sample do not depend on that sample's depth. Whether sample_01 changes any conclusion is answered empirically in T3S2 by a leave-one-out re-test, not asserted.

T3S1 scores all 50 human hallmark sets per sample with UCell on the vst matrix and repeats with singscore as a second rank-based scorer; agreement between the two is the robustness check on the score itself. T3S2 tests each hallmark score between inflamed and control with limma on the score matrix — 12 samples are the units of the test, not the genes — with BH across the 50 signatures, and reports effect sizes and confidence intervals alongside the adjusted p-values. With 6 per group the test is underpowered for small shifts; the report must say so rather than reading a null as absence. T1S3 collects the reproducibility record, including the hallmark collection version and the number of member genes present in the matrix for each set, because a set missing genes is a different set.
